utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First question, can everyone hear me? Mr. Harmon, can you hear me? Can you hear me, counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Great. Can the Registry hear me? Interpreters can hear me? Everybody can hear what is going on. The visitors' gallery? Everyone can hear what is going on? No technical problem? Fellow Judges hear me? Terrific. Now, Mr. Harmon, we can proceed with Colonel Karremans' testimony and I would ask the usher to bring him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. COLONEL THOMAS KARREMANS, recalled. Examined by MR. HARMON, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, good morning. You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine, so we shall resume with your testimony. You have been called by the Prosecution in the case of the Prosecution against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Colonel Karremans, yesterday you described the Bosnian Serb Army blockade that slowly strangled the enclave as a convoy of terror. What effect did this have on the occupants in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to stipulate some things which I have said yesterday concerning the circumstances, I must say the miserable circumstances, for the inhabitants of the enclave, but also for my own Battalion. That could explain something on the circumstances up to 6th July. Those, let us say, miserable circumstances in April, May and June were caused, what I said yesterday, by refusing the incoming convoys, either for the battalion or by UNHCR for the refugees. Thus, we had to do with a strangulation of the enclave or, so to call, an isolation, a total blockade. That meant for the population, for instance, that their situation was poorer than poor. There was starvation for the refugees. Some died by the starvation. There was no medical treatment at all for the population, no doctors, no dentists, no medicines. The Medicine sans Frontieres, MSF, was not able to fulfil its job in the local hospital. We could not do anything about infrastructure to support the local authorities like housing, like generators, power and electricity and water supply for the population. It ended up, for instance, that hundreds of inhabitants of the enclave lived literally on the garbage collection point. There was no travel allowed both for the population and for the Battalion. What was agreed in the beginning in 1993, so-called freedom of movement, there was no freedom of movement at all. Our conclusion for the inhabitants, the population of enclave, was that the situation was hopeless, inhuman and a lot of suffering for the people. On the other side, for the Battalion, I would like to describe that a little bit too, if I may, and I use a couple of parameters which I also put in my reports for the higher echelons and also for my national authorities. In the first place, the logistics, I have told you, your Honours, a little bit about that yesterday on the diesel, the lack of diesel which implied that we have to live in the dark with my Battalion for a couple of months. We had no electricity for water, for heating and the weather conditions in those days till the end of May were extreme, a lot of rain day after day, so we cannot use our vehicles, on one side, because of a lack of fuel, but on the other side, the roads we had in the enclave we could not use them. Because of the lack of diesel, we had to patrol by foot with all the consequences of the mines all over the area. There was no possibility of resupplying my observation posts and that is why we used horses from the locals. What I said before, there was no heating especially under those extreme weather conditions. We had no medicines. We had no spare parts, we had no engineer equipment and no food except our combat rations and we lived on combat rations a long time. We called that at the end a "logistical regime". Then on my own personnel, the soldiers, I had a lack of personnel because they could not enter the enclave as of 26th April. They got no mail from home. There was no freedom of movement. We could not leave the enclave. We could not enter the enclave. The third parameter were the operations. We have adjusted the orders for the Battalion several times (and I explained that yesterday) from eight observations posts to 12 and even 13 at the end, patrolling by foot instead of using armoured personnel carriers. We made contingency plans as of, let us say, the air strikes in Pale at the end of May. Contingency plans were for the observation posts one hour notice, and one hour notice meant that the soldiers on an observation post after an order should leave the observation post within an hour. That was 24 hours a day, the time we have been there. Humanitarian support, I just explained that to you, we were not able to support the population within the enclave. One of the other parameters was the psychological effect on the soldiers, but also on the population, the morale of the Battalion but also from the population. The terrain conditions were bad and the weather conditions were even badder. That ended up with 25th May that I informed in a long report to all the higher echelons and to the national authorities that I was not able to fulfil my mission any longer. That meant the end of the mission, period. Then we started with making all improvisations. Using those improvisations, we could handle the mission more or less until 6th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, based on the Bosnian Serb blockade and its effects as well as the capture of 55 of your soldiers by the Bosnian Serb Army, did you feel you had the means to fulfil your mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the end. In the beginning, when we started in January, I could fulfil the mission based on the mandate, based on what I had, personnel, equipment, the incoming convoys, but at the end of my stay over there, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention to the actual invasion itself. What was the effect on the civilian population once the invasion started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you know, your Honours, the invasion started on 6th July. It started with heavy fighting in the southern part of the enclave in the direct vicinity of OP Fox Trot, and by shelling the city of Srebrenica itself, the compounds and some other observation posts, but actually it started in the south. In the southern part of the enclave, there was the so-called Swedish shelter project, a lot of housing built under Swedish authorities. In that Swedish shelter project there used to live about 3,000 refugees. As soon as the attacks started in the southern part, all those refugees flew in the northern direction towards the city of Srebrenica. You can imagine there was panic, chaos in those days, what I explained before, no food and there was no way to give them houses in Srebrenica itself -- panic, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did the people flee to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They flee to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they flee to the UN compound in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the beginning. That was, I think, on 10th, on the Monday, and of course at the last day, on Tuesday 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many refugees were in and around the UN compound in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but that must be hundreds at the compound and maybe thousands around it. They were all guarded together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to those refugees in the compound around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have to refer to the 11th, the last day?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because at that day and the days before Srebrenica itself was already shelled quite some times and at the 11th, well, while all those refugees were guarded together, at least most of them, the BSA started shelling the city. It started shelling the compound of Srebrenica itself and that ended up with a lot of wounded persons, death. Also, in the morning and on the morning of the 11th, we already evacuated the local hospital and we brought all the wounded persons to the compound of Potocari. As soon as the shelling started in the afternoon of the 11th, just before the air strikes or during the air attacks, all the refugees flee into the direction of Potocari, in the northern direction, to the compound of Battalion staff and staff company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Colonel Karremans, some of the BSA artillery shells landed in and around the UN compound itself in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that cause civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That caused civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned as a result of the attacks on the city of Srebrenica itself there was a large exodus of civilians that fled to Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the refugees who fled from the UN compound in Srebrenica flee to the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately, how many people gathered in and around the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just an estimation, of course, but we were forced to split up the group of refugees because there were so many thousands. We put, let us put it that way, or "invited" is a better word, we invited about 4,000 to 5,000 refugees within our own compound of Potocari and then it was completely full, filled up, with refugees and our own personnel. Then we had another 15,000 to 20,000 persons still outside of the compound of Potocari and we used two or three shelled factories just in the vicinity of the compound of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the percentage of women to men in the 25,000 refugees that you say congregated in and around the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About those 25,000 refugees, most of them were women, children and elderly people. I think, and that is what I have stated before, there were about two to three per cent men between 16 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please describe the general conditions that were present in and around the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The general conditions from the people, the refugees, it is what I explained before, was poorer than poor. They had not had food and water supplies during the six days war over there. They were in a very bad condition, and we had no means to supply them, only by the water we had left into our own compound and some food and some medicines left, but the general condition of the people was miserable, more than miserable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Amongst those 25,000 refugees, were there some pregnant women who were delivering their babies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were, what I heard later on, there were five pregnant women with their little babies. What I heard was that one man hung himself during the stay over there and life was, let us say, going on during the two days that we had all those refugees around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Now I would like to turn your attention to air strikes. Can you please describe those air strikes to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. As everybody knows, I have asked several times for air strikes, looking to the mandate, the mandate which asked in the beginning of the establishing or the establishment of the safe areas of Srebrenica and Zepa and Gorazde, that one needed about 40,000 soldiers for that, and that was diminished after negotiations to about 8,000; that they changed the mandate in that sense that they combined it with air strikes or, let us say, close air support, air support in general. That was one of the parts of the mandate, and that was what I am referring to, that as soon as the attacks started on 6th, I asked for a close air support because one of OPs was attacked, UN troops were attacked, the city of Srebrenica had been shelled. There was no close air support available on the days that I have asked for that, except at the last day, on the 11th, on the Tuesday. I have asked that in the very early morning. I expected that at 6 o'clock. I had a meeting during the night from Monday to Tuesday with the local authorities and the military authorities. We discussed that even, and told them that we expected air strikes or close air support in the very early morning on 11th. That did not come. It did not show up. Afternoon, about 2 o'clock, the air strikes started. It had no effect on the population. It had no effect on the mission of the Battalion because everybody knows that the air strikes or close air support was too late and too little. It had an effect on the way General Mladic reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before I get to that point, let me just clarify one point with you, Colonel Karremans, was it your understanding when you were the Commanding Officer of the Dutch BAT unit in Srebrenica that air support was supposed to be a significant part of the protection measures available to you and to the population of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. You mentioned that there were air strikes and that they were too little, too late, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What effect did those air strikes have on General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The effect was that through the hijacked soldiers, about 30 in Bratunac, on one of the BSA kasserns over there, Mladic or one of his officers used the communications equipment of the vehicles over there, and ordered me to stop immediately using air support; and if that was not the case, if I was not able to stop that immediately, he should use all this weaponry -- that is what he told -- to shell the compound of Potocari, to shell the refugees within and around the compound and kill the 30 hijacked soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did General Mladic have the ability to deliver on those threats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could, he had the ability, because he had guarded a lot of weaponry around the compound on top of the hills like mortars, two main bell tanks, artillery and, what I explained already yesterday, the multiple launch rocket system from different types, all in direct side or direct direction of the compound and he could use that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, he had already used that on the UN compound in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to turn to another topic now, Colonel Karremans, and that is meetings you had with General Mladic. Can you explain the circumstances of your first meeting with General Mladic and explain when it occurred and where it occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The first meeting I had with General Mladic was on Tuesday night at half past 8. I was notified by my OPs room, they got a message, again through the same communication systems, that I had to show up in Bratunac for a meeting. I did not know what kind of meeting that should be, but I expected with somebody from the BSA, maybe Colonel Vukovic or Nikolic, or whatsoever. I was not before in Bratunac, but my LO liaison officers had a couple of times been there talking about trade, about military options with the BSA, so they came with me, two liaison officers. We went to the hotel in Bratunac and there was a crowd of military persons all in combat wear, gear, and clothes. There I met for the first time General Mladic. I did not know that he was there. I have not met him before, not in life, and there was also General Zivanovic, the Corps Commander of the Drina Corps. We were all standing there at half past 8. There were a lot of press around, television, and General Mladic started accusing me of all things what happened in the last six days, that I was responsible for the air strikes or the air support, killed some of his people, soldiers, that my soldiers had tried to kill him because of shooting at him, that we were not able to disarm the BiH forces within the enclave and so forth and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While he was addressing you was he speaking calmly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was shouting more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we got our famous glass in our hands, water.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you describe how that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we just got a glass of something in our hand and did not toast with that, but the circumstances were, if you can imagine, bad at that time because we too did not sleep for five nights and had not had hardly no food, no water, lived in shelters and bunkers. So we were all, let us say, not well for the meeting like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a camera crew present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a camera crew present and they put everything on tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After the glass was put in your hand, were pictures taken of you and other Dutch officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did that meeting last, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not too long. I think three three-quarters of an hour. I was able to explain the poor situation of the refugees which I did. I asked him for supply of food, water, medicines, and then he said to me, "You will have to, you should return for a second meeting at half past 11 just before midnight", I should take with me a representative of the refugees, if it was possible, one of the civil authorities of the opstina. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we went back to -- we left the hotel in Bratunac and drove back to the compound. The first thing I did there, I had a quick talk with my Deputy Battalion Commander and were desperately looking for a representative of the refugees. One of my officers knew and he saw him, that the head or the director of the secondary school of Srebrenica was amongst the refugees within the compound of Potocari. We found him and we explained the situation, that I have had a meeting with General Mladic and that he ordered, more or less, me to bring with me for a second meeting one of the representatives, a representative of the refugees, and asked him if he was willing to go with me to that meeting, and he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you then return to Bratunac that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to Bratunac that evening just before midnight, with my same two liaison officers and with Mr. Mandzic. Mr. Malic was the representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who were the representatives of the Bosnian Serb Army at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More or less the same which I met in the first meeting, General Mladic, General Zivanovic, there was an interpreter, which I referred already to yesterday, Mr. Petr, a couple of BSA officers and one or two civilians who I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At that second meeting did you request permission for convoys to pass through and ask permission for some form of relief for the refugees who were in and around your compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you please describe that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second meeting was a little bit more friendlier than the first one, I must say, and I was able to explain again the very bad circumstances and the situation in and around the compound concerning the refugees. Again I asked for support on medicines, water supplies, food. The wounded, I had about 100 wounded persons in the field dressing station, all in shelters. He made note of my requests without saying if he could do something about it. Then he started with his demands in, let us say, a kind of monologue. He asked me and also the representative of the refugees, Mr. Mandzic, that all Bosnian soldiers should lay down their weapons and deliver those weapons in the hands of the BSA. He said that he had a clear attitude towards the BiH soldiers, survive or disappear. He asked me and the representative to come back the next morning at 10.00 to have a third meeting. He promised that there will be a cease-fire which I had asked for until 10 o'clock the next morning, Wednesday, and if there will not be any support of the BiH in delivering their weapons, action should be taken by him by again shelling what he stated before of the compound and the refugees. He told something about Mr. Izetbegovic, the President of the Muslim people in Sarajevo, that he killed more Serb people during the last years than the Bosnian Serb Army did. He stated that he was not willing to use power against women and children. He asked me if Naser Oric -- Naser Oric was, let us say, the commanding officer of BiH forces -- if he could show up, I mean, if I could take him with him for the next meeting. I explained to him that we have not seen Naser Oric since April. He has not been back in the enclave since April. He stated that he was prepared to take over the about 100 or 110 wounded persons, and he guaranteed that if he had taken over or should have taken over the wounded, he guaranteed that they would have the same treatment as what is normal for treating the wounded, according to the Conventions of Geneva, Geneva Conventions. Again he stated or said or demanded that we should come back the next morning with a delegation of the people, a delegation of the refugees, and if it was possible, the civilian and military authorities from the enclave. Again he stated that handing over the weapons by BiH soldiers would mean survival of them; "If they should keep their weapons", he said, "that will be their death". He stated that if BiH soldiers should hand over their weapons, that they will be treated according to the Geneva Conventions, and he stated at the end that the destiny of the Muslim people was in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he also make any statement with regard to whether NATO or the UN were capable of guaranteeing the existence of the safe area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he quoted some words on that subject, but that he already did in the first meeting. I would like to say a meeting, between brackets, he stated that UN forces in general were not able to fulfil, let us say, the arrangements made by the cease-fire agreement and the UN resolutions as of 1993. I refer to the demilitarisation of the enclave. He said that in the first meeting and also in the second meeting that "Your United Nations forces were not able to fulfil their mission".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After that second meeting did you return to the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We did return in the middle of the night -- I think that meeting lasted one-and-a-half hours in total -- went back to the compound of Potocari. I had a telephone call with sector north-east; told him what happened that day, what happened during those two meetings, what was the demanded by General Mladic. Then we started looking for more representatives to have them prepared for the meeting on the next morning. I had a long talk again with my deputy, with some officers of the Battalion staff, how to find those specific persons and at the end we found them, we found a woman and one other person. So I had next morning three persons for the committee of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the next morning there was a third meeting, is that correct, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third meeting took place again in Bratunac, the same hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately, what time did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was more or less as the second one. The same persons, at least most of them, which I met in the second meeting and there were some civilians as well attended that meeting. I did not know them. They were introduced, but I cannot remember which jobs they had. They were all from Bratunac and Zvornik. He started welcoming myself and the liaison officers and also the committee of three persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "he" are you referring to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic, yes. Then the two other, let us say, the new representatives were able to introduce themselves shortly, started with the woman. She made some statements, very clear statements, towards General Mladic about the very poor, bad, miserable circumstances of all the refugees; that refugees were not responsible for what happened in the enclave during the last two or three years and that women and children were not responsible for those things which have happened. She was the representative of all women and children. They were all civilians and no military and no politicians. Also, the men introduced themselves and he asked for help and he said and stated, not blaming the refugees, and that they need a lot of things which I have already stated, had already stated before, like medicines, food, water and other supplies. He said that neither he nor my Battalion staff or myself were able to make contact with the Bosnian government during that night to ask for specific points for that third meeting, which meant that he was not able to lean on mandates or on other things to explain to General Mladic. After those statements of the two other representatives and Mr. Mandzic was already invited to tell something about himself during the second meeting, the day before, General Mladic started his monologue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you describe that monologue, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very long monologue. He started with a piece of history. In 1992, that the Bosnian Army, the Bosnian soldiers -- and he blamed Oric specially for that -- that they killed a lot of Bosnian-Serb families, soldiers, civilians, that they attacked a lot of villages in the surroundings of the city of Srebrenica, devastated a lot of villages and that, according to that and what happened in 1993, as soon as those safe havens or safe areas had been established, that the destiny of poor people was in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs. That was one of his other statements, he said it was too late for help, help either by the Bosnian government or by the UN troops. He said that there was a lot of misery in the last years, that the BiH forces within the enclave had murdered a lot around the enclave by raids looking for food, revenge, looking for revenge, terror. He stated that he was willing to assist refugees, those 25,000 refugees, but that he needed assistance, assistance by the local civilian and military authorities, from which I already explained that they were not available at the moment, not within that group of 25,000 refugees. He again said regarding the BiH forces, the same expression as the day before, "survive or disappear". He again requested to the BiH forces to hand over their weapons, even criminals amongst them could hand over their weapons. The second subject he stated was that the guarded population in and around the compound had the choice either to stay in Srebrenica or to be evacuated, to be evacuated to Serbia, to the Bosnian territory around Tuzla, or even to foreign countries. He said that the whole former, at that moment, former safe area had been encircled by his forces and that fightings should stop. We could hear that during the night before and the day that there were still fights and attacks going on. He stated that he was not able to assist the refugees as long as fights were going on. He stated that BiH forces could hand over their weapons in the presence of UN forces, UNPROFOR, he stated in general. I think he meant Dutch BAT. He stated that he was willing to assist with the evacuation. That was the first time in the third meeting that he used the word "evacuation". Then he stated that there used to be a good life in and around Srebrenica and in and around the vicinity of Srebrenica, and that he liked to have the same situation, that good life before 1992, that he would like to have that situation back. He said that, looking back or referring to that lecture in history, he did not like to kill what happened in 1992 and 1993. He, as a professional soldier, had no joy in killing either civilians or military. Again, he offered his help and the committee of refugees should think that over, think about how they could assist in the evacuation. He asked for our basic needs, I mean, what did we use, what did the refugees use, concerning food, water, medicines, medical support and so forth. He asked again how many refugees there were and we answered again 25,000, around 25,000. The committee stated that most of the refugees liked to go to their family and be guarded together with their husbands, and he stated that nobody should be forced to be evacuated. On the other hand, he said that if NATO air strikes or air support should be the case in other areas in Bosnia, that he should use his weaponry again and taking sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain what he meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same what he said or stated in the first meeting and before the first meeting, that if air strikes should occur again, that he should shell, let us say, the compound and the refugees in and around the compound. He said he would like to see all the men between 17 and 60. I asked him, and also both the men in the delegation, "What for?" His answer was that he would like to see all those persons because he said, he stated, there were a lot of war criminals amongst them and he would like to speak with them. Again, he asked if we were able to come in contact with soldiers whom Mladic knew. He was referring, of course, to Naser Oric, which I explained him before that he was not available, and some other persons, let us say, the commanding officers of the BiH within the enclave. Again I told him that there were no BiH soldiers available at the moment. So, there was no possibility to look for him because we were guarded together with all the refugees in a very, very small area. I mean, the compound and the two or three factories just in the vicinity of it and we lost our eyes and ears in the rest of the enclave. So we were not able to pick up those military representatives. Then he stated in his monologue that the BiH soldiers had only 24 hours to hand over all the weapons. After that statement, he asked some very specific conditions of the refugees. He stated that if he was able to assist, he preferred in a kind of priority to look for the weak persons first, for the wounded persons, and later on the rest of the refugees, women and children. He said that nobody should be hurt and that co-ordination and co-operation with UNPROFOR, Dutch BAT in particular, was one of his priorities. What I just stated, that he mentioned "evacuation" during his monologue for the first time, he asked for diesel for the evacuation. You can imagine that I started laughing a little bit because he was exactly aware of what I had for diesel; there was none, nothing, nil, and that I was not able to support him by giving him diesel. He said that his forces, BSA forces, will give escort during the evacuation. I said, "No, if there should be an evacuation anyway that my own Battalion should escort the evacuation". Then I explained to him in which way I should execute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your proposal to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My proposal was to put on every vehicle one soldier, not knowing how many vehicles that was. As soon as the evacuation started the same day, at 3 o'clock -- I think we come to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will come to that a little later in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was unable to do that. I was unable to put on each vehicle one soldier. Then he said that, and it was quite a remarkable expression, that Allah will not help, was not able to help, and Mladic could. He gave his word. He said to the commission not to be in panic, not to be afraid, and asked them to send that message to the refugees. I have asked again when that was possible, what happened or what should happen with the men between 17 and 60. He again said or stated that there were quite some war criminals amongst them, and that he liked to investigate person by person what they have done and what kind of persons those were. At the end of that meeting, all of a sudden, he started something to tell about the evacuation again, and he proposed, let us say it in that way, he proposed, that Kladanj should be the point for evacuation. Kladanj is a small village just on the border between Bosnian-Serb territory and the Bosnian territory around Tuzla. In fact, Kladanj is the first Muslim city in that area. Repeated, he repeated that within 24 hours all soldiers of the BiH, even in uniform or not in uniform, even war criminals amongst the BiH forces, could hand over and should hand over the weapons. He said, "It is better to live than to die". Then he referred to something what I said again, what I have said already yesterday or explained yesterday, that he knew everything what was going on in the enclave, what happened in the enclave day by day, and that he had persons in the enclave who informed, who informed them every day. So he was well aware of what was going on. Then he showed to us at the end of the meeting a book, there was a book of the opstina, a book in which marriages were assigned by people, marriage, and that the last marriage was on 29th June. He had as a piece of remembrance, I presume, a thing from, let us say, the entry of the opstina. He ended with something to say to the woman of the committee, that she was a fine woman, that she was open, or had been open, in the way of statements towards Mladic, and he did not say anything to both male representatives. Last but not least, he asked us, urged us, finding contact with the BiH forces and to convince them to hand over their weapons within 24 hours. That was, I think, the whole meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What time did the meeting end, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about noonish, about 12 o'clock, because at 12.30 I had a meeting in the compound with the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What time did the first transports arrive to take the refugees away from the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said during the third meeting, I forgot that to say, that the evacuation should start about 1.00, but it was not well organised in the beginning, or efficiently organised, so the evacuation started at 3 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So three hours from the conclusion of your meeting with General Mladic transport arrived inside in and around Potocari to start take refugees away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What type of transport arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of buses, I think 20 or 30, vans, big lorries and small military vehicles. I think the first evacuation was about between 40 and 50 vehicles and that was also, let us say, one of my decision points to change from one soldier at every vehicle to what we have done later on, put two vehicles with officers to escort the evacuations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, as a result of the number of vehicles, you realised that you did not have enough troops to put on one soldier per vehicle to accompany the convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So did you formulate another solution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We formulated, indeed, another solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Describe that solution, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That solution was that we should escort each convoy by two vehicles, two jeeps, seater jeeps; in every jeep one officer or non-commissioned officer and a driver with communications up to Kladanj and then they should return and pick up, let us say, the next evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to those escort vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first escort or in the first evacuation, I put my personnel officer, a captain, and one of the liaison officers. They managed to go with all the persons in that convoy to cross the border in the area of Kladanj. The vehicles left in the convoy returning to Srebrenica which disappeared and that happened with the other vehicles during the next evacuations too, and totally or in total 14. They were just picked up en route either by BSA forces or irregular forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I understand clearly, the first escort vehicle made it to Kladanj, is that correct, or made it to a point shortly -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six kilometres ---

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- from Kladanj because there was a barricade, a barricade, between the two borders and that meant that all refugees and later on also wounded persons were forced to walk, struggle, I might say, the last six kilometres to the border of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did any other of your escort vehicles make it to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them in the beginning ---

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but they did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. So, what happened to those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were hijacked, stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to the equipment that was used by the soldiers who participated in those escorts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same, weaponry, their personal weapons were stolen, helmet, flack jackets, private belongings were stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the consequence of losing those vehicles in relation to the convoys that left your compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The consequences were, I think, three-fold. In the first place, again we changed the way of escorting those convoys by putting en route, and the route was about 50 kilometres, four different points, let us say, contact points, so that the vehicles standing there on fixed points could see convoys passing, counting the amount of vehicles. What we did in the beginning as soon as a convoy left, let us say, the road in front of the compound, we counted the amount of vehicles and gave that to the first fixed post, so they could have a look and to control if the same amount of vehicles were still in that convoy. The second thing we did is that I ordered troops just outside the compound to work either in groups armed with their helmet and flack jackets or if they work individually, like the soldiers, the doctors, etc., that they should work just in a t-shirt without helmet, without flack jacket and without weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because in the beginning, especially for individuals working between the refugees, they have been stolen from the BSA soldiers around, there were not so many. They stole the helmet, personal weapons and flack jackets, just by pointing a weapon on the head of the soldiers and said, "I would like to have it, give it to me". They did not do that when groups were working outside, then they did not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you again see General Mladic on 12th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on Wednesday, yes. On the moment that the first convoy arrived, let us say, the empty vehicles, and turned around in front of the compound, and the first refugees were escorted to all those buses, vans and military vehicles. General Mladic appeared with his own vehicle and all his officers around him and some bodyguards, of course, and the press was there available too. They made all nice pictures of him and what was going on over there -- a lot of publicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with General Mladic on this fourth meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a short conversation with him about the evacuation, about what he stated in the morning, that first priority should be the wounded persons which he had stated, "Yes, that is correct, we should do something about it. Bring them over to the hospital in Bratunac". Then I said, "No, we do not do that, they stay here at the compound in our own hands or they should be sent or brought to NORMEDBAT Corps", that is the Norwegian medical Company in Tuzla, "escorted by either the Norwegian company or by the International Red Cross".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue your description of the fourth meeting with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was so busy during his stay there with the press and impressing his soldiers and the officers around him and talking to some refugees that I had hardly no chance to talk with him longer than, I think, those five minutes and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was your next contact with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next contact was the next morning, on Thursday, Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again in front of the compound just on the opposite of the gate, main gate -- again a short meeting. There was no press available or present, I must say. He had only a Colonel Jankovic with him and Major Nikolic, both officers of the BSA and, of course, his interpreter, Petr, and some bodyguards. He offered me, that was on that Thursday morning, offered me that we could go or leave the compound with vehicles after or during the evacuation of all the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In other words, that the Dutch Battalion could evacuate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told them that I did not like the idea of leaving the compound because of a couple of subjects. One of the subjects was that I still had some military on OP Alpha, one of the observation posts was still occupied. The officers and the soldiers from the day before escorting the convoys were still underway, I missed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In other words, they were still missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were still missing. I was faced at that moment with 55 wounded civilians within the compound, and I referred to the talk we had before, that I like to bring them over either by NORMEDBAT Corps or by the International Red Cross; that I had my Bosnian local workers on the compound, I mean, interpreters from the Battalion, interpreters from the United Nations military observers which I had on the compound, that I had all the people of the MSF, Medicine sans Frontieres, with me on the compound and that if we leave, we leave altogether but after some arrangements concerning the wounded persons had been made. That was my answer. He agreed with that and that is why I stayed in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there any other significant matters discussed at that meeting or did that conclude the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That concluded the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: By the end of 13th July, had all the refugees been deported from the Potocari compound area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I will look at my notebook. At 1600 on Thursday, the last refugee was gone outside the compound, and then one started with the evacuation of the 4,000 to 5,000 refugees which were able to stay within the compound. It started at 1600 and it finished about 7 o'clock. That was in three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the end of that, at 7 o'clock, then there were no further refugees in and Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no further refugees in and around Srebrenica -- I mean the compound at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was the next time you saw General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next time when I saw General Mladic was on the day of our departure, on 21st July. It was on the Friday morning. We had eight days to prepare our own, let us say, departure, to rest. On Friday, the day after the evacuation, all of a sudden a convoy with food, a lot of food, a lot of diesel was accepted and came to the Potocari area. So, then we had, from that day we had food enough, diesel enough, medicines, and we had eight days to recover from what happened in the weeks before. I saw General Mladic on the Friday and he invited me through his, I think it was, Colonel Jankovic that came to the compound that morning on Friday morning or Petr, the interpreter. He said that I was invited with my liaison officers to that same hotel in Bratunac where I had my three meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We drove to that hotel -- it was one vehicle -- with my liaison officers. There was General Mladic with a crowd of officers, most of them I knew already from the meetings. My own -- that is not the right expression. The Chief of Staff of BiH command, General Nikolaj, was there, a Dutch General, and his military assistant. They offered us a breakfast and we had some talks over a couple of things, about the weaponry. I asked him again what happened with my weaponry and that I would like to have it back. I knew already that we should leave at noon towards the Serbian territory and then the way up to Zagreb. Again I asked, "Where are all my vehicles? I would like to have them back with me". Then he said after some general things, but I have forgotten those, that he would like to visit the compound, look to our own convoys, how we did that, the vehicles. He asked me to have a talk with the soldiers and that that should occur at 11 o'clock, whether that was possible in the time frame. It was not possible. So I told General Mladic that it was not such a good idea talking to soldiers, not such a good idea visiting the compound, but he insisted in visiting the compound. He said, "OK, I will not be there at 11 o'clock. I will be there escorted by the Chief of Staff of BH command at 11.30". I left the hotel. We went back to the compound of Potocari. I had a quick talk with my deputy, seeing everything was arranged for our own travel with everything which has been left. That was the case, and I asked my deputy, "Are we able to start at noon?" He said, yes, he could. I told him that General Mladic would come. He said, "OK". We went back to the gate and he was already there before half past 11. He was held up by the commander of the guard, a very broad Sergeant. He could not go around that Sergeant. He was held up. General Mladic had a quick talk with him and then it was half past 11. I took him with me to my own briefing room within the compound, had a quick talk -- I think 20 minutes -- about some general things and then I asked him two specific questions. One question was, "What will happen with my equipment?" I told him what equipment I lost during the last two weeks. All my field vehicles, the amoured personnel carriers, a lot of personal arms, machine guns, the equipment of most of the observation posts. That was the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His response was that he should sort that out. He was in contact with his Ministry of Internal Affairs and they should do that in close combination or co-ordination, let us say, with BH command. He referred to the presence of the Chief of Staff of BH command. My second question, which I can remember asking him, was, just a general one, I asked him what should happen or should have happened if during the stay of United Nations troops in the safe areas of Gorazde, Zepa and especially, of course, Srebrenica, what will happen if BH soldiers were disarmed totally, completely demilitarised, if they should not have executed raids outside the compound -- outside the enclave, if both civilian and military authorities should live according to the 1993 regulations, arrangements, and cease-fire regulations. Then he answered that he, at least that was his answer, he would not have thought about attacking the enclave. He said it with a smile, more or less, and that was also more or less the end of our discussion there in the briefing room. Then we went outside to the entry of the compound, gate, main gate of the compound. The guards were changed. My guards went back to their company. Everybody in their vehicles and exactly at noon we started leaving the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, thank you very much. I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have concluded my examination of Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Let me look at fellow Judges. Judge Odio Benito, I do believe you have some questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, after leaving Srebrenica and Potocari, where did the refugees go in these convoys, buses and trucks you have explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, all refugees which I explained left the safe area of Srebrenica within an amazing short time -- that was Wednesday afternoon and Thursday, the whole day -- and they have been evacuated to the Kladanj area, the one, the first, let us say, Muslim city in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: To the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the confrontation line, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to them during the travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because they stayed in vehicles. That was one of the things I would like to do in the beginning, to put a soldier per vehicle, to have a look what was going on in buses or trucks. They did not inform me what was going on in buses because we did not have any use for that. The only thing we could do, and that was the second option, just escorting those big group of vehicles, convoys, by two cars in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But your vehicles and cars were stolen by the Bosnian-Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What did your soldiers do after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, because you had soldiers in those vehicles and they lost the vehicles, the helmet, everything, but what did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were guarded together during that night, the night of Wednesday and Thursday, by the Bosnian Serb Army, or the irregular part of it, I do not know exactly. They were guarded together, I think 12, in total, or 14 officers and soldiers. They stayed over night two times. Some were along that route, the route from Bratunac to Kladanj. They were fed by the Bosnian-Serb Army. They could shelter, for their own protection, they said. On Friday they returned through Bratunac to my compound.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you or any of your soldiers see Bosnian Serb soldiers beating, killing, raping he refugees in or around Potocari in those factories you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, they did. In some cases, refugees had been beaten and as soon as one of my soldiers noticed that, they stopped with it. I got two reports from my soldiers on Thursday after I met General Mladic; one report referring to an execution of one man and a second report about an execution of nine men from which they found the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be presenting evidence in regard to both of those incidents described by Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): Did you ever ask General Mladic during your meetings what happened to the people, refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because the last meeting I had with him was on 21st. That was eight days later on. We were not aware of what happened with the refugees. I mean, in general, I know -- I knew that they were all evacuated to Kladanj area and afterwards picked up by the Pakistani Battalion and by the International Red Cross, by the Norwegian medical Company. They build tents, shelters, supply points for the refugees. A part of them has been transported to the air base of Tuzla and other parts of the amount of refugees were transported to other facilities. That is the only thing I knew, and I did not discuss that with General Mladic at all.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Would you say, Colonel, that you received adequate support you asked for from your superiors? During those difficult days before the fall of Srebrenica, you told us that you asked for support.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you receive that support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can expand on that days and days, of course. That is why I was lucky that I could explain yesterday and in the beginning of the morning what happened with the inhabitants in the enclave, the refugees and with my soldiers. We had our daily SITREPs, our daily situation reports, in which we wrote everything what happened that day, what we need for supplies. Besides that, I reported at different times, several times, I must say, on the level of north-east command in Tuzla and the BH command in Sarajevo, what I needed to fulfil my mission. I was specific in that, exactly what we needed, medicines and food, diesel, etc. I asked for support many, many times during our stay over there. I know that there have been many discussions on all levels, above the level of the Battalion, sitting there with the population isolated in an enclave like Srebrenica, but we did not get any support at all.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I am going to ask you a last question and ask for your personal opinion, Colonel. Looking back, would you say that the United Nations and NATO did its best to help people to save their lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the one hand, yes, if we should have had our freedom of movement which was one of the points of the NATO, United Nations resolutions of 1993, and we could travel forth and back to the safe areas, in general, and to Srebrenica, in particular, for my Battalion but also for the International Red Cross, the other non-governmental organisations like the MSF, the UNHCR, and we were able to assist, help, the refugees, I think the answer is yes; but because of the strangulation and because of the isolation and not having had support at all, then the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Strangulation and isolation ordered by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I now ask my other fellow Judge if he has any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, throughout these, perhaps, five meetings you had with General Mladic, did he ever take into consideration your demands or was it always, as you said, a monologue and he did not respond to any of your objections or claims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had, let us say, three major meetings with him but meetings between brackets because, in my opinion, a meeting is two directions. A monologue is not a meeting. Indeed, those were monologues. In the second meeting, I was able to explain the bad situation and he made even notes of that and that was it. In the third meeting, on Wednesday morning, the woman and the other men of the committee could make their statements. They made note of it and that was it. So, the conclusion, only monologues, no two-way negotiations. He did listen to my requests, if I may say so, but did not support them at all. He had his own line in negotiating or in telling what he would like to tell, and what he would like to do.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you express any disapproval of his method of separating men, as you said, between 16 and I think 60 or 65 from women and children? Did you object to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, your Honour. I objected to that already in the meeting when he said that, by asking, "What is the meaning of that?" His explanation was what I stated before, he would like to have the men between 16 and 60 to look if there were war criminals amongst them. Maybe he thought that all the Bosnian soldiers were war criminals. He did not explain what he would like to do with them except that he wants to speak with them all.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he ask you for information about these people, to give him any kind of indication where they are and who they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, your Honour, he did not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: He did not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So there was absolutely no way of knowing about them through your Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In your last meeting with him, you said it was on Friday morning, by that time it seems that you had already known about the executions you mentioned. Were you aware of everything that was happening and the way the refugees fleeing away were treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think not at all. The information in those days confirmed the information about, let us say, the military side of what was going on in the Battalion, resupplying, what has had to be done before our own evacuation, if I may say so, and last things, what happened during our week that we stayed there and negotiations between some of the officers of my Battalion staff and some of the BSA soldiers on wounded persons -- I had still one of the Colonel surgeons in Bratunac in the hospital, to look what was going on with the wounded persons over there. We had discussions about the diesel because on that Friday after the evacuations I got a lot of diesel; what we should do with medicines and food. They were more or less the subjects we discussed in a couple of, let us say, small meetings, not with General Mladic (because I have not seen him after the evacuation), but with his officers. I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But did you include any mention, not to say protest, against the executions or the things you heard about in this last meeting you had with him, and what was his response if you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not protested in the last meeting because I even did not expect that meeting. I was not aware of that, because we became a message through our communication systems, the OPs room, that had to show up, let us put it that way, again in the Bratunac Hotel; and sitting with his whole crowd over there we had, he was again a little bit monologue-ing, and asked me how the Battalion was and how we were doing and if we were prepared to move and ready to go. There was hardly no opportunity to evaluate, let us put it in that way, what happened in all the weeks and days before. To be frank, I have not thought about the idea of asking him what happened with the refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: According to you, he was present all the time and he was aware of all that was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was present during the six days there of the attack and invasion of the enclave -- at least I presume. He was present during the evacuation. He has been there two times, which I explained, and if he was not there, he was in the hotel in Bratunac which he used as command post and the kassern in Bratunac which he used as command post for, let us say, the other things he had to do concerning Gorazde, Zepa, and I do not know what. After my last meeting with him, a short meeting on that Thursday morning, I have not seen him before, or if I have not seen him afterwards, except that I got some orders from the higher echelon about our own travel to either the Kladanj/Tuzla area or to Zagreb. That was still a point of discussion on the higher echelons. One asked me if could, let us say, come in contact with General Mladic, to discuss that, because nobody had contact with him since the evacuation, nobody from the higher commands. So I got, let us say, some notes by fax, made a small letter about it and sent that to his interpreter, Petr, who lived in Bratunac with the request to hand it over to General Mladic and ask for a response. I got a response, I think, on Friday, the same Friday, when the first convoys with food and diesel came in. That was the only contact on paper I had with him. In his reply or in his answer he said, "Yes, I will take your requests concerning your leave whenever that should occur and your requests on the lost equipment", he said "lost equipment", not "stolen equipment", he will take that into consideration, and asked me to have patience. He should have a meeting with General Smith on Sunday and I think that occurred on the 19th, and in that meeting he should discuss the leave of Dutch BAT, and then he should come back, let us say, to make all the arrangements for our leave.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You speak of evacuation and you mentioned that several times he asked you to assist in this evacuation; that means really the deportation of the people of Srebrenica to the Bosniak site. This deportation, although you did not assist, was very highly organised. You said that buses came and everything was very minutely organised. So, this was the headquarters of Mladic who did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. It was -- I think he ordered that himself and what I stated before during many briefings and also hoping that everything was prepared, preplanned in advance. Also, the massive crowd of buses and vehicles, and I always use an example in northern western countries, if you like to have 30 or 40 buses, then you have a challenge, but in a country like former Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, to gather there 30 or 40 buses you are not able to do that in one day. That must be preplanned a long time before. So, he had a plan and he executed that plan more or less minute by minute or day by day. He ordered for the evacuation. He asked for assistance of the Battalion but not more than -- you will hear that from the next, I think, witnesses -- assist the people to go to the buses, prevail or prevent, I must say, panic, chaos and supplying the refugees as much as I could with water, food and medicines -- at least what I have left over. That is the only assistance I could give.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mentioned that 55 soldiers were taken into custody by the Serbs, I think it was on 6th July. How were they treated and how long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not on 6th July. On 6th July, on the Thursday, let us say, the invasion started, the attacks, or, yes, the attacks started, and the fights between both parties. In the southern part of the enclave also by shelling compounds and the city of Srebrenica itself. It ended up on Saturday, two and a half days later, on the retreat of OP Fox Trot when one of my soldiers died. After that, let us say, Saturday afternoon and Sunday and Monday, he picked or he attacked a lot of observation posts by using force, weapons and soldiers, encircled them and circled them and take the soldiers hostage and took them with them. He guarded at the end 55 of my soldiers at two points, one in Bratunac, in the northern part of, I say north of the enclave, and one in Simici, south of the enclave. At the end, after the evacuation, they were guarded together, all 55. I had a talk with them, not with all 55, but with the 30 persons staying in Bratunac. I asked in the first meeting I had with General Mladic if I was able or allowed to speak with them. "Yes", he said, "you are able to do that, you are allowed to do that". I had a small talk with the soldiers, asked them if they were treated well. They said "yes", they were treated reasonably well. That same applied which I heard later on already being back in Netherlands to the other 25 soldiers from Simici.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mentioned several times that you raised the matter to the higher echelons, your higher echelons. Was there a prompt response or did they leave you just to your fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking to the circumstances in that time and knowing that both commanding officers of the north east command and BH command were not available, so I had to do with both Chief of Staffs, my direct superior was, of course, the Commanding Officer of north east command in Tuzla. What I did is, on every time when I think it was necessary in shelters and in my own offices or in the communication centre of the Battalion staff, I had direct communications with either north east command or BH command. We did report, we did make our reports verbally, at least I did it -- it was one of my responsibilities -- to the higher echelons and we did it every day at 6 o'clock by the daily situation reports on paper, by fax. The conclusion, my direct superior in Tuzla, but also the command in Sarajevo, were well aware of what was going on and what happened minute by minute in the enclave, every day of our stay over there. Again, asking support, logistical support, in the weeks before or even which I have stated before, close air support, no. The support was worse.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I would like to ask you also, in one of the meetings and you mentioned Major Nikolic, he stated that all Muslims should leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That was at an official meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- no. We had a sequence of meetings with both parties, not together. We tried to have them together around the negotiation table; my predecessor did, he was not able to that, one or two times. We were not because of the quarrels, because of the fights, over and over. So we had every week a fixed meeting with the civil authorities, with the military authorities, within the enclave and also with, let us say, the Commanding Officer of the Chief of Staff of the BiH forces. We should have a meeting, a fixed meeting, every weeks with the BSA outside, either on OP Echo or on OP Papa, but that was not the case. Meetings with the BSA was always when we liked to have that or when they liked to have it, very irregularly, and it was one of those irregular meetings that I was involved somewhere in the middle of February, if I can remember, that I met Major Nikolic and it was at that meeting that he stated what I said yesterday, about Muslims killed half Assembly during Second World War etc. and that he hated Muslims and, in his opinion, the Muslims should leave the complete territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have some very short questions I would like to put to you: the troops you talked about, where did they come from? What was their composition? You talked about the fresh troops that arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We were -- no. Around the safe area of Srebrenica there were three brigades, the so-called Skalani Brigade in the south, the Bratunac Brigade in the north and a third Brigade in the west. Those Brigades belonged to the regular army of the BSA, the regular Drina Corps, but those three Brigades consisted of elderly soldiers, soldiers from that area, an area where they belonged. As soon as on 6th July the invasion started or, let us say, the attack on the enclave started which, General Mladic stated later on, he used three new Brigades, one in the south and one in the east and he had one in reserve in the north. That means that he did not use the regular forces around the safe area of Srebrenica. He especially used other forces which we have noticed two days before 6th July. In Bratunac, there were a lot of battle noise and there was a lot of noise about moving tanks, artillery, military vehicles -- all those moves which we have reported on a regular basis and in our daily SITREPs.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think there were any militia, fresh people, fresh militia, in these forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, what I have heard, just I have heard, I have not noticed that myself, that the so-called Arkan Brigade was involved as well. That was a Brigade with, let us say, special forces from the BSA but, personally, I have not seen them during those six days and during, let us say, the evacuation of refugees. That could be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The evacuation with the Dutch Battalion, was it possible in the plan with your superior, was the Dutch Battalion asked to provide that assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the assistance, your Honour, for the evacuation of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I am talking about the evacuation. You have talked about a meeting with General Mladic, I think it was the second or third, I cannot remember, where all of a sudden he said that had you to proceed with the evacuation. That seems it was not tackled during your first or second meeting in Bratunac. So, I had the impression that you were not surprised; you knew that there might be an evacuation or did you decide, as the superior, that the evacuation would take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first two meetings, I did not have a clue what was going on about the destiny of the refugees. Knowing that we had about 25,000 refugees in and around the compound, one of my major points was to ask support as much as I could get from the BSA, what I stated before, food, water, medicines, a good arrangement for my wounded, for the wounded refugees, about 100 or 110. That is what I have asked for during the meetings, the first meetings, with General Mladic. In his third meeting, he started to talk about evacuation, and that was a surprise for me as well. We arranged a committee of the refugees to co-operate with them about what should be done or what should we do on the circumstances under which those refugees were there in and around our compound, what could we do as much as possible and we needed a committee for that, to talk about it. I used that committee -- I mean in a nice sense of using it -- I asked them if they could assist me as much as possible, at least to respond on the questions and they, that committee, went with me to the third meeting. That was the meeting in which General Mladic stated or told about the evacuation. I was as much surprised as everybody was because the meeting was at the end of the Wednesday morning and at 3 o'clock Wednesday afternoon the evacuation started already. So I was confronted with something new, an evacuation of 25,000 persons. Then you have to think quickly -----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. I heard what you said, but what I am trying to find out, faced with that surprise, you were surprised, you said, the refugee committee is surprised; did you have adequate time to ask your hierarchical structure whether you could proceed in such a way or did you have sufficient freedom to decide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no time to -- I had time to inform my higher echelons which I have done, which I did. I asked several times for what could I do, how could you assist me, what should I do? No answer on that. There was no policy in that either. So I could, let us say, do what was the best thing to do at the moment and knowing what time was left between that third meeting, and 1 o'clock was mentioned by Mladic that the evacuation should start, that we were complete surprised, everybody, that such a thing could happen and that he already had organised such an evacuation. I was not able to do anything about it, and that was why we decided -- I decided in the beginning -- to put on every bus or whatsoever a soldier. That was the least thing I could do, and assist the refugees as much as possible going to buses by giving them food, water and medical care and look for them during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank. My final question: if you talk about the list, we talked yesterday to the investigator from the Prosecutor. It seems that there was a list of men in an age range which I did not quite understand. Can you very quickly tell us what happened with this list of men, what was their age and what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had, as you know, your Honour, 25,000 persons in and around the enclave, almost all women, children and elderly people. We estimated about two to three per cent men, men between 16 and 60, more or less, and we did not know how many men there were -- in general, we knew -- how many men there were outside the compound. We have asked through the interpreters and through the committee if it was possible to note or, yes, set on a piece of paper all the names of those persons, male persons, between 16 and 60 within the compound. There was no time left to do that for all the other persons. There is one person who has asked me in the past, "Why have you not put the names of all the refugees on a piece of paper?" You can imagine, your Honours, that that is not possible. What we have done is we have put the names of men within the compound on a list, and what I can remember, 239. There were about 70 which did not like that and they have not done that. We have done that on purpose because we like to know what could have happened with those persons. What happened with the list, the lists have been faxed to Tuzla and to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Fine. Colonel, the Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony. Last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Colonel, did by any chance General Mladic's office get hold of this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about the answer I should give now, because there are two possible answers, and maybe one of the witnesses after me could answer that question.
