There are two possible answers. One said or has stated that one of my officers offered or handed over that list to one of the BSA officers at the gate. Some others said, no, that was not the case. I am still at this moment not aware of what was going on with the list towards the BSA. I do not know. I cannot answer the question, do or does the BSA, or did the BSA receive that list of persons? I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ask the officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, based on the numerous questions we put and once again thank you, Colonel Karremans, to have spent so much time with us. But do you have any wish to add any supplementary questions or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Colonel, in this Mladic/Karadzic case, we have finished with your testimony and we will now finish until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We would like to call our next witness, Lieutenant Koster. LIEUTENANT KOSTER called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Lieutenant Koster, do you hear me? Do you hear me? Please take the statement which has been given to you and read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly I declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think my first question would go to the Prosecutor and he will introduce you to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Lieutenant Koster, would you please state your full name and spell it for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last name is Koster, I spell K-O-S-T-E-R.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a logistic officer and an infantry soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In the Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Dutch Army, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Have you been serving with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you please tell the court where and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served in Srebrenica and that was January 1995 till July '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When did you start, you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In January. Was Colonel Karremans your Commanding Officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What was your position with the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My position was to be the Logistics Officer of the Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just give us the outline of your duties in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had to manage all logistic affairs, although we had few means and, well, that meant very strict planning and distributing our logistic affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where in the chain of command were you placed in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a staff officer and my direct Commander, my Logistic Commander was Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you on duty in the beginning of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on duty in Potocari, inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Inside the compound, so your working place was inside the compound mostly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK. You were there even on 11th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was also outside the compound then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Will you tell us about what happened after the fall of Srebrenica when refugees started to arrive in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was on 12th, sorry, it was on 11th July, we were ordered to go outside and to form a unit to receive the refugees, so we went outside and made a hole in the fence from where we could guide the refugees towards the compound. When we were posted outside, approximately at 1500 hours the refugees arrived in a few and small groups at first and, well, most of them were women and children and older women and older men. They were terrified, they were afraid, looking for help, and when we were there, well, we could not tell them what to do at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said that you formed a unit to take care of the incoming refugees. How big was that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, approximately 30 men at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were you in command of these 30 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said you opened a hole in the fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Is that the way you led them into the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were not allowed to let them in by the main gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the road which led from Srebrenica to Potocari was constantly on the direct sight, in direct fire from the Serbs. For example, when the days before, when we left the compound by vehicle, we were fired upon with mortar fire and that kind of thing. So, it was better for the people to take another route and another way to the compound which was more covered by trees and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: They opened that hole in the fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When people started to arrive, the first ones who arrived, did you show them all in into the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed at first. We first showed them the way to the large buildings of a former bus station where bus repair and bus maintenance was done, and we told them to take cover inside of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you are saying that you were not allowed, allowed by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By my Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What was the kind of shelter you gave them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What kind of shelter did you give them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The big buildings of the former bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was outside the compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then when did they start entering the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was later on that day when the total amount of people was going to be a big crowd, we were ordered to let the people through the compound in small groups of 25 persons, and send them through the hole in the fence to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How did these people arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, like I said before, at first in small groups, later on there was one big mass of people coming down the road from Srebrenica to Potocari and, well, they came with a big noise, women crying, children screaming, children also crying. Well, people were in terror. They came down the road towards our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: On foot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On foot, yes. When we could receive them, we just only could tell them to wait and to stay at our position. We could not tell them what to do and they were keeping asking these questions from, you know, "What are we going to do?" or "What are the plans for now?" They were very much afraid of what was going on with them, what was going to happen with them, but we could not tell them, so ..... They were -----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Had they walked the way from the city of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them. There were several vehicles from the compound in Srebrenica to the compound in Potocari carrying some wounded, but when they started to move, not wounded people picked their places and also in every spot of the vehicle where they could hang on, they got a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you are talking about these vehicles, were they the UN vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were our UN vehicles, yes, trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No other means of transportation like buses or trucks for these fleeing people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some APCs for medical aid. Those APCs were also carrying some kind of wounded people and some healthy people towards our position and moving people toward the compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: They started coming in small groups and then they grew more and more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you make estimations, looking at what time they started and then how they slowly encompassed a big crowd of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, I was ordered to make a rough counting of the people constantly. Well, it started by with 10 people, then hundreds of people and then even more thousands of people. Well, it started approximately, they started coming around about 1500 hours and, well, until late in the evening it stopped. So, for example, the road had a diameter of six metres and was fully crowded with people, most of them women, children and older men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When you said you started to count them, did you do that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and later on that day I compared with my colleagues to make a rough counting of the total number of people and we came to a number of approximately 15,000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 15,000 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15,000 people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many of them were led into or brought into the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on top of the 15,000 there were 4,000 to 5,000 people let into the compound. So, at the end of the day, there were 15,000 outside the compound and 4,00 to 5,000 people inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We are talking now about 11th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did they stop coming in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they stopped and there were -- the crowds stopped. There were a few people coming down the road still, but the big mass, the big mass of people, the big crowd, stopped coming towards our position, yes, and it was fully filled with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What did 30 soldiers do to care for these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, during the day I ordered for some reinforcements because we could not stand any longer to hold the people. We had some interpreters to make it clear for them what to do and, well, what we were doing down there was the best we could; give them some medical help, telling them that we would guide them and escort them and guard them and protect them for the best we could. Well, whether it was help, any help needed, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That with 30 persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I ordered some reinforcements, so later on that day I guess it would be 50 to 60 men outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What kind of medical support could you give them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly first aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Like bandages and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we had some, yes, some bandages. There were several wounded men and women, also women giving birth to children at our place. We also had some assistance from MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: MSF is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Medicine sans Frontieres. So, the wounded we could give them only the first aid because we did not have more means outside, also inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What about giving them food and drink then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, outside it was impossible for us to do because we had so scarce means of food rations and all that, so we could not give them any food outside the compound. From what I have learned later on is that we made a soup of food rations mixed, mingled with water for the people inside the compound. Outside the compound, some people were carrying jerry cans and bottles of water, carrying water with them. Nearby our position, there was a small well where people could get some water, so that was -- it was needed because it was tremendously hot that day, so water was a very needed factor over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So the people inside could get some soup to eat or drink, but outside could you give them anything at all, apart from the water from the well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you paint the picture of what it looked like when night fall came? What did it look like in and around the compound then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was like being on a scene. It was a little bit surrealistic. Being outside, these people, I slept outside, also my men slept outside. We did some patrolling that night. We had some posts to protect them. Well, the big noise stopped, all the screaming, etc. and all the shouting and crying stopped during the night, although little children kept crying on and the noise decreased, so ... but it was very surrealistic being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were there any attacks from the Bosnian Serb Army or any soldiers or units attacking this amount of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not in person but we were fired upon with mortar fire during the day. Well, the shelling was not among the people, well, it was very close, close firing, approximately 50 metres from our position, among the houses nearby our position the explosions of the grenades and the mortar grenades came down, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But these crowds of people were not shelled or fired at directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not directly, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then you said you had some 30 people and some reinforcements; what about the rest of the personnel of the Dutch Battalion? Where were they deployed during this time? What I want to know is how many persons, how many soldiers, of the Battalion in total were present in Potocari when this flood of refugees arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it should be approximately 200 men, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 200 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Where were the rest of the Battalion deployed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were assigned to the OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: These are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Also, part of them were located in the compound of Srebrenica, but most of these men and women were supply forces, so they were not fighter men, they were not infantrymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But the ones you are talking about in Potocari were fighting men, infantry soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few of them, yes, but most of them were supply forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Most of them were supply forces. Were any of your personnel taken hostage or assaulted during this day, the 11th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK. Could any of you have any rest the night between 11th and 12th July last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for me personally, no. For the most of them, I guess not because you were busy helping people, doing some patrolling outside the compound among the people. Well, maybe you could get an hour or two sleep, but, well, it was not such a rest. You could not rest very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Will you then turn your attention to the following day and give us an account of what happened on 12th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the morning it was relatively quietly. The people, well, they woke up and started asking questions about what was going on, and what we were planning to do and what the Serbs were planning to do, so we could not tell. We carried on giving them medical aid; still wounded people came down to our position, asking for a doctor, asking for medical help; still women were looking for their children like the day before because they lost their children in the big crowd of people; also children looking for their families and that kind of things. That carried on all morning and also the sun also appeared again, so it became tremendously hot again that day. Later on that day, approximately at 1300 hours ---

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- 1300 hours, yes, we heard a noise of tanks and APCs, and I heard by radio that there was a tank and an APC coming down the road toward the compound. So the people, well, there was panic and the people were scared and they ran down to the south of our location, and so we had to wait what was going on then and wait for the Serbs to make a move.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they did they came to our position and also to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You are talking about the army, the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. They came to our position and we made a demarcation line of some red and white tape over the road and, well, they stayed behind the tape. Some of them asked for the commanding officer at my location, so that was me, and he introduced himself and so did I. I cannot remember his name. I asked him what he was planning to do and he did not tell me. Well, after that he turned his back on me and went down to his forces. At that time there were, well, approximately 20 to 30 Serbian soldiers at our position at the road. Well, their action was just walking around looking at the people, also shouting at the people, asking questions. I had an interpreter next to me so he could translate what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of what they said to the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most of the times they were mocking at them, and doing that it was a very odd situation because they sat down on the ground and started to begin singing, and they also -- they actually did not make a move. They were just staying over there at their location behind the red and white tape probably, I do not know what to do. So we just could stay there and wait what they were going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on that day, Major Nikolic came down also to my position and he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you know him beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised him from photos in the Operations room. Well, he wanted to have a look among the people and he wanted to walk through to the other end of our location. At that time it was reported from my southern post, which was the last units of the Bravo Company, that also at their location some Serbian soldiers arrived. Well, we escorted the Major Nikolic with our liaison officer and an observer and he walked down through the people. After that, he returned and also the situation stayed the same for a couple of hours probably. Then one of the commanders came to my position and told me that he would bring a vehicle loaded with bread for the people, and that we should make way for this vehicle and it really appeared and then they started to give bread to the people. They also had a camera team accompanying them and the camera team, well, they were filming while they were giving bread to the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many people did get some bread? Did they have something for everybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. There was a very small truck and, well, they were throwing the bread and giving the bread to the people. My interpreter told me while they were doing that they were shouting at the people again and mocking of them and calling them names. Well, the vehicle returned for one more time also loaded with bread, and also a fire truck came down to our position to give the people some water and, well, one by one women were allowed to leave the crowd and to fill up their bottles with water. Everything was filmed by the Serbs. Then the fire truck disappeared again. Later on that day, should be approximately at 1600 hours, more troops came down to our position, more vehicles, more jeeps, more civilian vehicles. At one time my interpreter told me that he thought he had seen General Mladic, and General Mladic came to my position. He introduced himself and so did I. He asked me who was the commander in charge. I asked him what he was planning to do. Well, at first, he did not tell me nothing and he walked right through our line of tape and towards the people. At that time, of course, I reported to my commanding officer and I was told that I should send Mladic to the compound, to Colonel Karremans, so he could talk to him, but he would not do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He would not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Who would not, Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So you asked him to go and talk to the commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He said no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said, "No, I am doing what I please to do and I am in charge here and nobody tells me what to do, and I am outside here, and you will see what is going to happen". He told us to co-operate or else there would be -- we were, you know, told to co-operate with him; we would be best off by co-operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You said "or else", did he -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we would be best off by co-operating. Those were the words said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. Go on with the story, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he went to the people and he spoke to the people not to be afraid; he should, he would take care of them. He was talking to little children accompanied by a filming team, a camera team. I was constantly protesting that he should go to the compound. While doing that, some buses arrived and I reported that. Then I asked him again what he was going to do and he was irritated, and he told me that he would evacuate the people to another place. At once some of the Serbian soldiers pulled down several of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They pulled down and pulled away several of my men who were holding the civilians and, well, the Serbs told the civilians to go to the buses, to get inside the buses. Well, at that time the situation was taken out of our hands and we could only escort the people and provide any harm of the people and they were fully in charge at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many Bosnian Serb troops were present then, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I estimated approximately 40, 50 men and, well, they were still coming up, more men, men with dogs, all that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You were outnumbered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were severely outnumbered, yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK, please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I was told to escort the people and to provide any harming of the people, and we could not do anything else than just escorting them, and the Serbs took over and they pushed the people to go to the buses and they kept on doing that till the buses were fully stuffed with people. They were putting far more people inside the bus than normally is usual. The buses drove away. Then we had to stop the people again and we had to wait till other transport arrived at our location.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you in any way convoy or send somebody with the buses when they went away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned later that we escorted the buses and the trucks by sending some of our men with a jeep driving in front with the buses. But, well, the first transport, well, they succeeded escorting them and the other transports, well, the jeeps were taken away from us and so we could not escort them any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: By the Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb soldiers, yes. Was any separation of sexes taking place before they were loaded on buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, they were looking for men, older men, well, men of fighting age, potential fighting men. They were separating them from their families and from the rest of the people. Well, they kept on doing that the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What happened to these men who were separated from their families? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put them inside of a house and, from what I have seen, they were just sitting there and waiting. Their personal belongings were taken away and put outside of the house and I only saw these men waiting. As far as we could, we were protesting against it, but we were, as you said before, outnumbered so we could not be at all places.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course. What about General Mladic, was he present when these things went on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I lost sight of him. When the first buses started to drive away, I lost sight of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This transportation of people started, as I remember as you said, about 1600?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the time when General Mladic arrived ---

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When he arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and, well, it should not be more than half hour or an hour later when the buses arrived and drove away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many bus loads of people left Potocari this day, 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not count them at all, but, well, they started -- sorry, they ended up when night fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: With night fall they stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many bus loads that was? Do you have any idea how many people left on the first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Half, a third, no idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no estimation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You can make no estimation. They stopped at night fall, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Still then people were inside and outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Was anybody taken out of the compound on this first day and put on the buses or was that people from outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, there were people from outside the compound because I was there. I do not know if people from inside the compound were taken outside because I could not see it from my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You could not see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK. Then night came; can you tell us something about what happened during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were told by the Serbs that we had to clear the road and to join the people on the terrain in front of the former bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Clear the road from the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The road should stay open because they told us there could be some transport moving to Srebrenica and from Srebrenica to Potocari. Well, we collected the people at that point and we stayed there patrolling during the night and the Serbs, they left. Some of them came back during the night and they were taking our arms, and also our vests and helmets and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you describe in what way they did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they joined, they formed groups of three or four men and then they walked up to a UN soldier and told him to give away his weapon and his bulletproof vest and his helmet and his equipment and when he refused that, he was forced to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: At gun point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally at gun point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many of your soldiers did lose their equipment in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Many out of these 30, 40 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That went on during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning of the night. Later on that night they disappeared and I did not know where they went. We were alone with these people and then they were very, very quiet. Well, we kept on patrolling during the night and, well, helping some sick people and also again wounded people who still asked for doctors, for medical help, and we had a doctor outside our position -- well, till the morning came.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK. Then we arrive at 13th July. I will now ask you to tell the court what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 13th, well, we put down four APCs on the road to make some of the -----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: APCs stands for the -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Armoured personnel carrier -- armoured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Armoured, yes, sorry -- to make some of them an artificial gate so we could guide the people in a better way. Then, at approximately 700 hours, the buses arrived and half an hour later the Serbs arrived, and then there were more and more troops coming down to our position and when -----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Again an estimation, if you can, how many troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least 50, 60 of them. Again they start again to pull away my men and to put the people inside of the buses and the trucks and that carried on during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Any attacks on you or your personnel during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard some shooting on the west side of the compound coming from houses and that kind of thing, but not in my position, there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did this separation type of handling, this thing, did that go on even this day? Did they separate men from the rest of their families or was that only on the first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it still went on that day and, for example, we saw a 19 year old boy being separated from his family and, well, we protested against it and the Serbian soldier, he was impressed, and let the boy go to the buses, but they carried on separating the men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That went on this the 13th July all day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I have seen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When was the place emptied of refugees or everybody evacuated, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will have to look it up, one moment, please. It was on 13th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 13th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What time of the day, can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to be approximately, at 1800 hours. I had to do my report at the compound and get some food and a few hours of sleep, two hours, and it was at 1600 hours when I reported to duty in the Operations room it was at 1830. I was told it was not necessary any more because all the people had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Even the people who were in the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except the wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Except of the wounded people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: They left the wounded people? What about the men who were separated? Were they still around or were they gone also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were also gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you see them go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because I was on the compound asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you see when the people were taken from that compound into the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You did not see that. Did you see or hear any violence during the 13th? Was there any shooting then or other kinds of violence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in person. We heard several single shots, like I told you before, and all we did hear some rumours, it was on 12th July, while I was reporting at the compound, we heard some rumours from people inside the compound that there was a place where they had seen eight or nine bodies laying down on the ground and on 13th July two colleagues of me and I investigated that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Was that in the vicinity of the compound -- outside the compound -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was approximately, well, 500 metres away from the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What did you find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came down to that place, we saw nine bodies laying in a field near to a river. We went up to that location and we took pictures. We did not actually investigate the bodies, but we saw seven of them lying down on the ground with their face down to the ground; two of them were lying on their sides, on their back. They had, well, the seven of them had a shot in the back, in the middle of the back, and we took pictures and we also found some papers. The bodies, they were dressed in civilian clothes and, from what I could see and could make of it, they were men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You did these findings on 13th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you hear some shooting you could relate to that incident, to these people's death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only heard the several single shots during the day, so that is only what I have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Did you see other killed people around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the morning, one man who hanged himself on the ceiling of a small building, but he was already dead when we released him from the rope.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Any other incidents of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So by the evening of 13th the place was empty, there were no refugees any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the compound, inside also, no, except the wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The wounded people. Did you see General Mladic more than these times on the 12th that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during the night on 12th and on the 13th, during that night, I saw him passing by our position sitting in a jeep and he moved up to Srebrenica, and later on that night he moved back towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So you saw him twice during that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You saw him twice during that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But he did not stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You did not talk to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He just drove on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: OK. Then when only the wounded people were left, what happened then? What did you do in the coming days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for me, personally, I picked up my job again as logistics officer and doing the things requested and waiting for us to leave the enclave, and we were making preparations for leaving the enclave because we did not know if we could leave with all our equipment or just by taking our personal belongings and then leave the compound. So I took up my old job.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As a logistics officer, you can certainly tell us how much equipment did you lose during these days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know the exact numbers and figures. We lose weapons, we did lose some jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How many jeeps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you make an estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You cannot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: APCs, we lost APCs, and we lost, well, equipment, soldiers' equipment and bulletproof vests and helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: When did you leave? When did the Battalion leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on 21st, on Friday, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The week after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A week after that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostberg. Fellow Judges, you have a question, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant Koster, you talk of 15,000 people coming from Srebrenica to Potocari looking for help, mostly, you said, they were women and children and elderly people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you expecting this exodus from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you in Potocari, you and your team, expecting this exodus from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were outside there to receive the refugees, yes, and we had expected to come refugees to our position. That was why we were posted outside.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you prepared for receiving them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- just being there and being posted there and doing the best we can, but we did not have the equipment or medical equipment or even enough food to receive them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Had you, your team, asked for help to your superiors or to the superior command or NATO or UNPROFOR to face this emergency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you receive any additional support for help before or after 11th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What happened with these people, women, children, elderly, wounded people when the Bosnian Serb soldiers arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sorry, you are only talking now about the wounded people?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: About the women, children, elderly people in Potocari coming from Srebrenica when the soldiers Serb soldiers arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were afraid and they were not harmed or anything by the Serbian people, from what I could see, outside the compound. Well, later on, the periods we were outside, they were put inside of the buses and evacuated from my position.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you hear about massacres committed by Serb soldiers against Muslims in and around Srebrenica, Potocari, Bratunac at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only learned on the Wednesday that there was a position -- there was a rumour about eight or nine bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After those days have you heard about massacres committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only when I returned in the news.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Colonel Karremans or anyone else say "no" to General Mladic when he ordered the evacuation of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that because they already started it when I was reporting it, so the situation was completely taken out of their hands outside.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But the refugees were under your support, under the UN support, under the protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So did you or your superior try to avoid that the refugees were taken out in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not possible to do it because we were outnumbered and we were pulled away, and then the Serbs, they pushed the people and shouted at the people to go to the buses now, but to get inside these buses so being outnumbered we could not do anything at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Lieutenant Kosta, you just said that you were outnumbered, completely outnumbered. In fact, you were in a state of helplessness completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you at any moment threatened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In person?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No, the whole group in your capacity, you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were just told to co-operate and that would be the best for us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, yes, "best for us" means that something would be worst; if there is something best, then something can be worst. You mentioned that Mladic himself told you, you had better co-operate, you are all right, and then he told you, "You will see what is going to happen"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mladic, among his visits, he told you, "You are going to see what will happen". You mentioned that from your notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still do not understand the question. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What did Mladic tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. Yes, he told me that and later on he told me that he was going to evacuate the people of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then you mentioned that you saw them separate men in fighting age from the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. Did you protest or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You did and what was the reaction to your protest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they let the men go with their families and their wives and, well, at the places we were -- we could not protest or where we were not located, well, we could not do a thing.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did they pick them just at random or did they have a list in their hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just at random.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Because there was a list of 200 and something people which nobody knew if it was given to them or not. Do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about that list, yes, and it was made on the compound, at the compound.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That list was made just to make sure and to inform the Serbs that we were watching them ---

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and keeping everything under control about what they were going to do with the men, and so by that list we were also protecting them, so we were checking them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So this list was made by your men, by the officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not. It was made by a committee of the refugees inside of the compound and -----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not to me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I mean, to -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, it was not given to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You do not know if it was given to the Serbs or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, it was not given to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was not. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Lieutenant, on the basis of what we have heard, apparently, there are some vehicles from the Battalion that escorted the jeeps, some jeeps that escorted the vehicles, so you did you have some jeeps that went along with the convoys. I take it that those jeeps came back, at least some of them came back, so you had a chance to see some of your men before you left the compound. What did your men tell you about what happened and were they aware of the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only learnt from that when we left the enclave. Before that, I was constantly being outside until the 13th and I did not know what was going on during these escorts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Because the jeeps that were doing the escorting did not leave Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them were already taken away at our main gate and, well, that is what they told me while I was doing my reports. Well, at least one of them made it through and hat was the first transport, but that is something I learned later when I left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When soldiers came back, because there was a gathering before you left the enclave, what did people say to one another? What did soldiers say? Did anybody tell you anything? Did they know nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Nothing was said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: They did not say anything about what they might have seen? They did not see anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because I was not speaking to them. I was too busy at that time doing my job as a logistics officer, so I do not know anything about that. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Fine. You got together on a regular basis with the reports about the meetings with General Mladic, or was there a compartmentalisation between the different levels of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can the interpreter repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you have any input about the meetings with General Mladic or was there no information tricking down at the various levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know what was going on. I did not know the exact details of the meetings with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostberg, we have no further questions for the witness. So, we could have the usher show the witness out? Lieutenant, the Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony which you provided on behalf of the Prosecution. Then the Prosecution can show in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just to organise our proceedings, we are going to spend one hour listening to the next witness and then we shall proceed to a recess at about 4.30. So, Mr. Bowers, once the witness comes in, please do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. At this time the Prosecution would call Corporal Groenewegen to the stand, please. CORPORAL GROENEWEGEN, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will be going through the interpreter. Can you hear, madam? Can you hear me? Can the interpreter hear the English interpretation? Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, first, you will ask the witness to read out the declaration, the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hereby declare to speak the truth, the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Bowers?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Corporal Groenewegen. Would you start by stating your full name and spelling it for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Groenewegen, G-R-O-E-N-E-W-E-G-E-N.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Corporal, you currently serve in the Dutch Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the court your current rank and your responsibilities and branch of service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this moment I am a deputy of the -- [I am sorry, the witness has to speak into the microphone. It is very difficult to understand] -- I am a corporal. I am substitute of the Dragon infantry group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Corporal, have you served in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the court the period of your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From July 1995 until July -- January 1995 to July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who was your commanding officer at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Who are you talking -- sorry. [The interpreter is telling the witness to speak into the microphone].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean group sergeant?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment it was Sergeant Mulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who was your ultimate commanding officer in the area where you were assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Lieutenant Schopman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you stationed in Potocari when you did your tour of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you assigned to Bravo Company there at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negative. That is the Charlie Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many Companies were there in the Potocari area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there other Companies within the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you describe those Companies, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the Bravo Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you describe for the court your particular responsibilities when you arrived in the Potocari area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That consisted of OPs, doing OPs, that is, doing patrols on foot, guard on foot, just being in the enclave occupying the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You have used the initials "OP", does that refer to observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You were serving as an infantrymen at one of the observation posts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you just tell the court, as an infantryman assigned to an observation post, what were your daily assignments? What types of things did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my work consisted of patrols of the OP itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there different types of patrols that you would undertake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you describe those, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two kinds of patrols, border patrol, social patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What were the differences in these two patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The social patrols were to have certain contact with the people and to overlook situation in the enclave; the border patrols was to see whether the fighting parties complied with the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time if we could have Exhibit 60, the map of Srebrenica enclave shown? Corporal, you were assigned to a specific observation post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have been at two actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What were the two posts that you performed your responsibilities at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mike and November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you please take the pointer and just show on the map the two locations of the observation posts within the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the map).

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If you could do that again? I do not think we had the map on the screen. Which observation post is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you show us the other observation post at which you served?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first months of 1995 when you arrived at Potocari, what was it like serving at these observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was quite attractive; the day consisted of patrolling, being on guard, resting, a patrol every other day, so we did not really have very much to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you encounter any resistance or antagonism from the Bosnian Serb Army in the vicinity of your patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At some point later in your tour of duty did the situation begin to change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That was the last month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened in the last month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started with a complete discontinuation of convoys, hence we could not continue our work because of lack of fuel, food.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In late June/early July of 1995 which observation post were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you describe for the court what started happening in the vicinity of OP Mike with regard to conduct of the Bosnian Serb Army in the vicinity of the observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from the Serb positions that we could see from our position, we saw people, soldiers, who made signals towards us that we had to leave the OP in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When did they start making these types of gestures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many soldiers were in the Bosnian Serb Army contingent that began making an indication for you to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 10 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that distance, we could not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did they yell anything that you could hear from across the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What types of things could you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We do know one local word used by the local people there and it means something like "shoo, go away", and that is something we could clearly understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How long did these initial verbal type of provocations last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did it occur on more than one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just experienced it one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Eventually, did the Bosnian Serb Army in the vicinity of OP Mike take any aggressive action against the observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mortars, shooting mortars towards the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When did the BSA contingent across from observation post Mike open fire, when in way of time of day and day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been 10th July, almost immediately after the threats themselves. That is when they started firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You were personally in the observation post when the Bosnian Serb Army began firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you remember what time of the day it was? Was it in the morning, afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you tell approximately how many rounds fell around the observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several hours -- about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many other infantrymen were with you at the observation post Mike when the mortar fire began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 of us then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did all of you do when the mortar fire started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They spent almost all day in the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you know if at the time the mortar attacks began on OP Mike there were any other attacks occurring on observation posts in other areas of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they also took place at other OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How could you tell that there were other attacks on other observation posts within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received that -- we received those communications from time to time and we could hear the firing throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You stated that the firing lasted most of the day, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly during the day time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was there still some firing that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hardly none.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: With your own personal situation, what did you do after this shelling occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in the bunker till then, that is, the OP personnel. After that we resumed our work as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was there any other interference the next day when you resumed your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The morning after that, there were some, there was some mortar firing. Towards the afternoon, I was taken down, down to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You returned to the compound because it was your turn, as far as a rotation of duty, to return to the Potocari area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Potocari compound, what was the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tense. We spent quite some time there in the bunker too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you returned to the compound did you have an opportunity to see any weaponry that the Bosnian Serb Army had in the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At some point later were you able to see any sort of their weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What was the time and what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would have been around noon, the afternoon. We saw the flames, constantly we saw the flames, of the rockets and we saw where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would this be a reference to a multiple rocket launcher of sorts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Where was the rocket launcher located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the nearest mountain close to OP Papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you determine what the targets were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No precise targets, most probably just provocation, so that the people, the population, would not move.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK. Thank you. After you returned to the Potocari compound, at some point refugees started arriving from the Srebrenica compound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is on July 11th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was Bravo Company also travelling with some of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we saw a very big group of refugees and then an increasing number of Bravo Company people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you have any responsibilities with regard to receiving this exodus of refugees from the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started to form a line from the compound to receive the people as best as possible and to move them in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many soldiers were stationed outside the compound in this receiving line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 30 to 50 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Once you were assigned to this receiving line, did you stay out amongst the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few refugees that arrived at our side of the river, indeed, we received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In fact, over the next several days you even slept outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you just briefly describe what you saw on July 11th when the refugees arrived, just briefly state for the court what shape the refugees were in and some of the sights that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose was to see to it that the refugees that arrived, they had to be led towards the compound, but it became clear very quickly that we could not have everybody moved, go there. So the rest of the people had to remain outside. As much as possible we placed them in the factories, in the buildings, in the vicinity. It was very chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the wounded get some sort of priority as far as being allowed into the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Women and children, as far as possible, were helped first and then men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: While you were on this receiving line, did you see someone inflict an injury upon him in an attempt to get into the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What was the weather like at this time when the refugees first started arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very hot. It was stifling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was there sufficient water and toilet facilities and food for the influx of refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to provide water as much as possible, jerry cans and barrels of water. We tried to bring them as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You have stated that the refugees arrived approximately on June (sic) 11th. What happened the next day -- I am sorry, July 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: July 12th, Serbs started evacuating refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were you out on the receiving line when the first soldiers arrived into Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: About what time did these first soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: That was on July 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: From which direction did this first group of soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From OP Papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 60 so that the Corporal can point that out on the map, please? Could you just show what direction the soldiers came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the map).

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK, so they are coming from the south to the north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The north to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: North to the south. OK. From the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Down towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK. Is there a main road that enters into Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, there was one. There was just one entry, the enclave, and that was at Potocari, OP Papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you describe for the court what type of soldiers these were that first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were not -- those are soldiers that did not wear the regular clothing; all kinds of camouflage clothing and head wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Heavily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were they armed in a standard military way or did they appear to have more weaponry than is normal for a standard soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is probably at random, whatever they wanted to bring along.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When this first group of soldiers arrived into Potocari, did you see or hear any firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Where was that occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly along the sides of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would that be up in the hills surrounding the Potocari village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I could not see any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you see houses catching on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that sounded like return fire or actual combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was just like some firing from one single party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How long did this firing along the periphery of the city last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact answer. It would be an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK. Can you give an estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the moment the soldiers arrived until night fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: After this first group arrived were there other soldiers that came later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Approximately, how long after the first group arrived did this second group of soldiers come to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you describe this second group of soldiers for the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sort of more uniformly dressed; almost all of them had the same uniform, plus camera crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers with dogs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK. The direction that the first group had come, was that the same direction as the second group that arrived into Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In your opinion, was there any way that this first group of heavily armed soldiers could have entered the city of Potocari without the knowledge of the second group that arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it looked like that the heavily armed group would go first, to be sure, and only after that the camera crews would follow, I mean, to record everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did it appear that they were acting in co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You mentioned camera crews. What were camera crews doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Small groups of people with complete camera equipment, sound equipment and photo cameras -- some men with photo cameras.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you tell what these people were filming or taking photographs of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
