utterances.text: Mainly the contact made by the Serbs quite quickly after having arrived and surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: By the time this soldiers started arriving on July 12th, do you know approximately how many refugees would be in the vicinity of the compound at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside or outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the compound about 2500, and outside the rest of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate of approximately how many were outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened with the refugees once the soldiers began arriving in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the evacuation actually started, the people were more or less left alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did they appear to be concerned when the soldiers arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You have mentioned that an evacuation eventually started. Can you give us an approximate time of when people started being evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How did this evacuation proceed? What type of vehicles were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards the vehicles, there were buses and lorries, trucks. It looked quite rough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How long did the evacuation effort last on July 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To night fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the evacuations begin the next day on July 13th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Approximately what time on July 13th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7.00, 8 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You were still out on the line amongst the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At this point in time, on the morning of July 13th, did you start seeing any type of separation effort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. As from that point in time, the men were separated from the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who was doing this separation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the Serbs that were there in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You watched this process at a fairly close range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were walking around in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you describe for the court how the Serb soldiers would separate a man from the crowd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly groups of three to four men. A maximum of one or two men were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was it always a situation where the armed Serb soldiers outnumbered the men that they were taking out of the crowd or the group of men that they were removing from the crowd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to the men that were separated out of the crowd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men were taken to a house that was nearby until that floor was full of people and then they were deported.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you see into this particular house where the men were collected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is that because part of the front wall was missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you observe this house throughout the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there all day but I did not constantly concentrate on the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: During the course of the day, did you see men brought to the house and then taken away from the house on a fairly regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. As soon as the house was almost full, if you looked up after some time you saw that it was empty again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: On the afternoon of July 13th, did you witness a killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Approximately what time of the day was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point if we could have the lights dimmed? We have a brief video to show. I believe that is Exhibit 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Corporal Groenewegen, do you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this house that is shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is this in the vicinity where you were when you saw the killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK, that is fine. Thank you. Now if we could have Exhibit 62 which is a still photo taken from this video put on the overhead? Corporal, if you could use this photograph and if we could move that up just a little, please, and then use the pointer and describe to the court where you were and what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day I walked around, essentially, over here and this is the house where I saw the murder being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there refugees in the general area here where you see the open space with the grass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should not be there. We were there in order to send them back so that they would be sent back through the ordinary route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did you see that day? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my position, the line where I was to keep people out who wanted to move towards the buses, I saw that a group of Serb soldiers from the crowd took one man, and then I did not take any notice of that any more and then later on I heard shouting. I responded, and it appeared to be the same group with a man that they had taken along.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK, if I could stop you a for one second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And after -----

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many men took the individual out of the crowd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were they soldiers, armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All four of them were armed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: The man taken from the crowd, was he armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did he resist in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Impossible. He probably knew what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: All right. Continue and tell the court what you saw after he was taken from the crowd.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment he was taken from the crowd, I no longer took any notice of them. Later on, when I heard the shouting, I looked towards them and I saw the same group, Serbs, with the man they had taken along, and afterwards around the corner he was shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When he was taken behind the house that appears on the still photograph, did you hear shouting from that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really loud shouting, but noise, a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you heard the noise, you turned and what did you see when you first looked behind the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the position where I was standing, I saw that the men gestured to the man they had captured, so to call, to face the wall. The soldiers themselves looked at one another for a second, as if they were asking each other, who is going to do it. One stepped out and he was about a few metres behind the man and shot him with an AK.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you tell from that distance where the bullet impacted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That must have been the head itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When the soldiers took the man from the crowd behind the house, were there some other Serb soldiers in the general vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them working around -- walking around that could see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How many were also behind the house in addition to the men that were responsible for extracting the individual from the crowd and shooting him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time of the murder, two at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: From where you were standing across the way, you could hear the gunshot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the two soldiers standing behind the house react when the man was shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment of the shooting they looked up in that direction, but then they resumed their own work quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: After the man was shot, what did the soldiers responsible for the shooting do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men disappeared behind some bushes very nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did they drag the body of the person that had been shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that moment, not when they disappeared behind the bushes and not afterwards either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the soldier use a single round to shoot this individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a single round.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: During the rest of the day on July 13th, did you continue to hear these single shots throughout the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the court how often during the course of July 13th you heard these single isolated shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 20 to 40 an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you determine approximately what area these shots originated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly from the house, the area with the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would that be up away from where the crowd of refugees was being kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, a lot further, in the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In your opinion, were these single round being fired in any type of combat situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Single shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: So that does not indicate any type of combat occurring, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At the time you were hearing these single shots, I assume there were Serb soldiers in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did they exhibit any concern when these single shots would occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Corporal, can you recognise General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How is it that you are able to recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the briefings beforehand, news, the situation in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you see General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When was that that you saw General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 13th July, throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the court some of the things he was doing during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw him speaking to his own people and our own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did he appear to be in charge of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: The day, July 13th, that you saw General Mladic in Potocari, is that the same day that you saw the Serb soldiers begin separating the fighting aged men out from the crowd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: The day you saw General Mladic is also the same day that you saw the execution of the man behind the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: It is also the same day that you heard the continuous repetition of single shots being fired in the area beyond the refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You recall the video showed the road running in front of the house where the execution occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is that the road that General Mladic would have travelled each time he arrived in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: We have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecutor. Do you have any questions or do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Corporal, you mentioned that you heard single shots repeatedly till night fall. Did you or did your Battalion enquire what it was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all had our own ideas about it, but nothing was done.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: "Nothing was done", do you mean that there was no protest or objection or contact with the Serbs to ask them what it was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we asked, then we did not get any reaction, so we did not get any answers from them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When this execution was undertaken at your site, was there any objection to it to the Serbians or did they draw your attention to what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment it was so chaotic that we were all very busy and we could not react as we would normally react.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to know why they selected a man like this man to execute him in public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecutor. I think we have finished with this testimony. The Tribunal would like to thank the Corporal for his testimony which we have got through the Prosecution in this present case. The Tribunal would also like to thank the interpreter so that we could hear the testimony of the witness. Could the usher please accompany the witness out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, I suggest that we adjourn until 4.50. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The court adjourned for a short time).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Ostberg, you have submitted an application to the Trial Chamber in connection with the protection of a witness. Now we today came out with an order on the part of the Chamber and we have ordered that the name, address, whereabouts and other identifying information concerning the person previously identified by the pseudonym Witness A shall not be disclosed to the public or to the media; that the name, address, whereabouts and other identifying information concerning Witness A shall be sealed and not included in any of the Tribunal's public records; that the pseudonym Witness A shall be used whenever referring to this witness in the Tribunal proceedings; that the testimony of Witness A be presented using image altering devices; that any discussions, should there be any, relative to the issue of protective measures for pseudonym witnesses shall be held in closed session; lastly, that the identity of Witness A also be protected while he enters and leaves the courtroom, which means that at present we have blocked off part of the room. We will see whether there are any other measures that need to be taken, and once we have seen to it that we have all the protection required we can remove this here blocking the view. I would like to know from, Mr. Ostberg, whether there are any other measures. There should be an embargo, as it were, on the images that are now broadcast live from our own channel that is available to all television networks. If you agree, I think we should, therefore, for at least 15 minutes block out the images in case one of us has a slip of the tongue. What do you think of that, Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, that is also my opinion, your Honour. So I think this delay also will take place. Other measures I do not require.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see. The Registrar would like to say something. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I would like to know for this last measure if the technical booth is ready to have a video delay at this moment, because I am not sure. I think they are asking for a 10 minutes delay to install this video delay, because they were not prepared for this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We shall, therefore, adjourn for 10 minutes. So that those following the proceedings will understand what the point is, this is so that the protective measures taken work, because they will not work if we do not delay by some 15 minutes the broadcast of the images. What you have to bear in mind is that the witness who is going to be entering the room might himself in his account say things that might reveal the disclose either of his identity or that of other persons. So it is not just in respect of this witness, but we also want to protect other potential witnesses. As I said, we shall adjourn for 10 minutes. I would ask the technical unit to do their utmost so that we can proceed with the hearing. (The court adjourned for a short time).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, I want to ask you that if the same clauses and measures are going to be valid for tomorrow we have to have this delay in the transmission of our images also tomorrow, so we must be prepared tomorrow. So, we hope that this information will be passed on to the technical facilities so that we will not have a late start tomorrow morning. You have the floor, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I call Witness A. Witness A called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, can you hear me? Take your time, take your time. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In translation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The usher is going to give you a statement which you must read standing up, if at all possible. Please read it, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, please be seated. We can draw the curtains up. First of all, I would like to thank you for having come here, for being prepared to come and give us your testimony. We are fully aware that this is something very difficult for you. I and my colleagues want to assure you that you can speak freely because you are under the protection of this Tribunal. It is an International Tribunal. Now counsel for the Prosecution -- there seems to be no sound in the public gallery. Can the public gallery hear the Judge? No. Can you hear the Judge from the public gallery? First of all, we also must bear in mind the public gallery. Counsel for the Prosecution, do you hear me? It seems there are some technical sound problems. I nevertheless note that this has happened once before. Each time we take protective measures for the witness it seems that our system of protection does not work and we cannot have the sound for the public gallery. This has already happened in a Rule 61 hearing and I regret this very much. We will not stay here inactive, so once again I have to adjourn the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can the public gallery hear me? Is the sound coming through? Counsel for the Prosecution, please proceed. I just want to say that we are very appreciative that you have come here. We understand the difficulties it has for you. You are under the protection of the Tribunal. Therefore, you can speak freely without being worried at all. Prosecutor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Will you tell us, sir, if you were present in Srebrenica when the town fell to the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you tell us what day that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on 11th July '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I would like to ask you if you feel comfortable to tell the Court what you experienced that day and the following three days without having me guiding you through the events. Are you prepared to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then please, sir, tell the Court what happened to you on 11th July and the days to come, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 11th July they came in the morning from the Civilian Defence to our village and told us that the Serbs are attacking with armoured vehicles from Zelen Yadar in the direction of Srebrenica. So, we were expecting, afraid and panicky, what will happen with Srebrenica. We listened to the news from Sarajevo wondering what might happen. Until about 2 o'clock in the afternoon two planes of NATO flew over. We heard detonations and knew that they were bombing. Around 3 o'clock we were listening to Sarajevo news, and they said that NATO planes bombed armoured vehicles of the Serbian Army, that Srebrenica will not fall, it will be protected, and so we relaxed a little and went after our business. Then towards the evening I saw people going from the village. I was in the field collecting hay with my family. I saw people going from the village and my wife shouts: "Look at those people, they are going", and we could see women and children and horses all on the move. I told them: "Let's go home, something new must have happened." When I arrived home all in my village were ready to go and they said: "What are you waiting for? Why aren't you coming? Don't you hear them say that Srebrenica fell and somebody has come and told us to retreat, so women, children, elderly disabled should go towards the UNPROFOR base in Potocarska Rijeka." So with my family I entered the house. We took the basic necessities, some food and something, and we started around 8 o'clock from my home. We went down to Potocari and there on the way we saw people sitting along the road. We said: What's happening? Why don't you go to the UNPROFOR compound?" They answered: "They are not letting us." So with my family I spent the night on the grounds of a factory called Mart 11th or Sacmar. In the morning some went to enquire what will happen, when will there be any transport, whether there will be any transport, and they come back and say: "We no know nothing. We don't know who will provide the transport. You will see when the vehicles come, then we shall take you." So the afternoon arrived until the first vehicles came to take people away. So, with my family I set off towards those buses with all those people. This UNPROFOR had blocked the road because the people were moving in a wide front, so they were not allowing those people to move the whole width of the road. They tried to narrow Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.Pages 740 to 764. down the passage, so that they could enter the buses smoothly. Passing by the UNPROFOR I saw some soldiers. The distance between UNPROFOR and buses was about 20 metres or so. I saw some soldiers also in camouflage uniforms and I saw they were all UNPROFOR. I could not distinguish the clothes. After all, I had never seen very many of them until that time. So I passed by this human wall of UNPROFOR, and another man in a camouflage uniform of UNPROFOR said: "Goran, hey, you old man", and then I realised it was not an UNPROFOR man but a Serb soldier. So he took me aside to the left, towards the side of the road and there were a few more people standing, and they kept separating. When they separated us some 20 of us or so, they said, "Well, here, you go to a house so that you don't stand on the road", and somebody asked: "Why are you separating us?" The answer was: "Well, don't ask. You are being ordered and do as you are told." So we entered a house, the ground floor of the house. The house was still brick, I mean it was not completed. We were there. Then they brought another group there. So, there were Serb soldiers around us, on guard around us. Then a Serb soldier said: "Do you know Ratko Mladic?" Some said they did know him. He said: "Who doesn't him will have an opportunity to meet him now." After a short while, and from the same direction that we approached that house, an officer appeared in our sight and he was escorted by another three or four soldiers. They came to the entrance door there at the ground floor. He said, "Good day to you neighbours", and some answered and said, "Good day to you." He asked: "Do you know whom I am?" Some were silent and some said: "Yes, we do." He said: "I am a General of the Serb Army, Ratko Mladic. Those who do not know me, now have an opportunity to see me." Then he said: "See what happened, what befell your Srebrenica. Even the NATO pact cannot save you. All their bombing of our forces was in vein. They can do nothing to us. Your Srebrenica fell today. Tomorrow Zepa will fall. Gorazde is going to fall the next day and then Bihac's turn is next", and so on. "Why have you followed Alija Izetbegovic? Why didn't follow Fikret Abdic?" Then I said: "I am not interested. I could not care less about Fikret Abdic or Alija Izetbegovic. What we do care about is why are you separating us from our families. Why can't we go with our families when we are all elderly and where we are not able-bodied men?" He said: "I need to separate some 180 of you because there are so many of our Serbs in Tuzla and some 180 of them are kept captive in Tuzla and then we shall exchange you." So he left us and went back the same way to the pavement. They continued separating group by group. Since not all men could fit into the house, they were standing in front of the house. Towards dusk those who were sitting in front of the house were then ordered to stand up and start moving in front of all soldiers. So they got up and moved. When they left we were then also ordered, "Come out of the house and follow them." So I came out and every 10 metres there was a Serb soldier with an automatic rifle aiming at us. He was shouting, "Quicker, quicker, faster, faster", that is all they were saying. So we descended towards the top of the UNPROFOR compound. There were two buses there on the road. In front of the buses there was a red vehicle, and the last bus in the road was full of people. So we boarded the first bus. Next to the first business Ratko Mladic was standing together with those three or four men, soldiers, who accompanying him. So when we all boarded the bus he came closer to the door of that bus and told the driver: "Close the door, follow the red car and off you go." So the driver closed the door of the bus and the red vehicle started towards Bratunac. The bus set off after the red vehicle and that is how we arrived in Bratunac to a hangar. That is where the bus stopped and there we were met by some 10 or 15 Serb soldiers. The door opened and they ordered us to get off and enter the hangar. We got off, entered, sat down and after a little while we heard another vehicle arriving, another group arrives. All the same people from Potocarska Rijeka were those who came. So until this hangar was filled to capacity and those Serb soldiers were at the door, they introduced themselves. They said where they are from and said some were from Serbian, from Valjevo, from Krupa, from Sabac, from Loznica. Whether they were or not I could not say, but at least that is how they introduced themselves to us. Other were villagers from Bratunac. So they enquired after their neighbours, Muslims who were there: "Well, how come that you are here? Well, are you all right? Where is your father? Where is your mother? Where are your brothers?" So I could so that they knew each other. So this Muslim asked them: "How are your people? Are they all right?" So they were engaging in these kinds of conversations. Now when this warehouse was full somebody on the outside said: "Twelve of you have to go tonight. Well, you have been ordered. Is that clear?" He said it in a very harsh voice and they all in unison said, "Yes, sir". Then the silence fell and then with a torch lamp one came and went around us and he asked: "Who is from Glogova?" There were a couple of people. Then he would go again with his torch lamp around and he would pick up one of them and would say, "You whom I have just lit with this battery, come out then." Then he would stand up and come out. As he would come out he would turn to the left from where we had come. From there one could hear some blunt instruments how he was beaten. Then he would start moaning, we could hear that, and then silence would fall again. Then he could come with the torch lamp again and find, would light another and take him out and again we would hear blows and we could hear moans. When it would stop, then the next one would come. Some would be beaten and he would be brought in still alive, brought by two men supporting him under his arm pits. He would bring him to the door and then one would shove him in the back and throw him at us. This person was beaten but still alive, so he would be drawn or pulled to a corner. That is what they did throughout the night. Sometimes they would make a short break and would then go on. So it went on until the morning. When the day broke out somebody said: "We don't have to keep them any longer, they're all dead." Then somebody said: "Well, if they are already dead, then take them out." So five of them are dead, some from beatings. So five dead people were then drawn, pulled out from that warehouse. Then they stopped killing and made a break. Then we heard some vehicles, some freight vehicles, some heavy vehicles approach the hangar. Then a man came and said: "I need some 10 able men to do something for us." Nobody volunteered. He was asking for volunteers but nobody volunteered. Then he picked out 10 men. He said, "You, you, you, you, you, come out." Then went out. Everybody was silent for a while. All was quiet and then we heard those vehicles starting their engines once again and leaving. Those 10 did not return. Then a tallish with black hair and said: "Let's see your belongings. What have you got? Come up with them here." So some people asked: "What do you want us to take off?" They said: "All that you've got, bags, papers, watches", and so on and so forth. So we all turned them over. Then he asked for money. He said: "Money, all the money." "What money?" He said: "All kinds of money, but basically marks." So what we had we began passing them from hand to hand, including German marks. When he collected all that he left. Then they started bringing water because we had asked for water. Then they started bringing water to us to drink. We asked also to go to the loo and we also were permitted to go to the loo. But they told us: "Listen, when you come out of this door you turn to the right, and there is a room and that's where you go, but coming out you have also to look to the right. If anyone is to look leftward he will never enter the hangar alive again. When you come back from the loo then you have to look leftward." That is how they started going out. I also went out around 9 o'clock perhaps, and they had already started taking people out and killing them again. I could hear some screaming. When we went to the WC to the right and then to the left they said "toilet" and that is where we went. So as I came out I looked to the side taking out, and I saw three or four men standing side by side, the one in front holding an automatic rifle and ordered: "Come to me, come to me." This man who was between those two, as he was coming up a man with an iron rod hit him on the head. So he fell and from the right-hand side another one hit them with an axe on the back. This had a sharp edge and the axe hit him and was there and he was down as a worm squirming. I turned my head to the left then and they went on doing that until about 4 o'clock. Then vehicles were heard, some heavy vehicles, arriving and then they again picked out 10 to go to do something for them. Again 10 went out. It was very quiet. Then later on again those vehicles left from that hangar. Then Ratko Mladic appeared at the door and we all started: "Why do you keep us here? Why do you kill us here? Why don't you take us away?" He said: "Well, we could not arrange for the exchange to carry out. If we could have organised the exchange so quickly all this would not have happened. Some of you are exchanged and now you are going to Kalesija for exchange. Except that one has to count you all to see how many of you are there, so that I can provide the transport for all of you." One of us stood up and counted us all and told him: "We are 296 of us here." He said: "Now I will provide transport for all of you." He left. Then we could again hear vehicles arriving there. They were arriving and then one said: "Well, come now, one by one the buses are here, so you are leaving." So we stood up and went out of the hangar. As we were coming out of the hangar we could see that the concrete was wet, that it was washed. When I came out I saw six buses standing. So, I boarded the bus of Centrotrans from Sarajevo. So we all boarded buses. There there was also one Serb soldier in every bus standing by the driver. The door closed and Ratko Mladic appeared on the left-hand side. Some 10 to 15 Serb soldiers were also gathered round him, and he was talking to them. He was telling them something but I could not hear what he was saying to them because we were closed in that bus. So he gave them some orders and then he left and we were still there in those buses. We asked the driver: "What are we waiting for? Why aren't we on our way?" He said: "I don't know. I was simply given the orders to come here and where we are going or whatever, I don't know." So we waited until it was dark. When the darkness fell the buses set off towards Serbia towards the Drina. We reached the bridge across the Drina, but we did not cross it. We were moving through Bosnia along the left bank of the Drina. We arrived at Drinjaca and there we were for about two hours in Drinjaca and then we continued towards Zvornik. We passed through Zvornik and when we arrived in Karaka near that aluminium plant or alumina plant we turned to the left. For how long I cannot say exactly. We arrived at a school, a gym, and there the buses stopped. There we were met by some 15 Serb soldiers, and we were ordered off the buses. We did and entered the hall. It was empty. There was no one there. It was a basketball hall. It was a hall where basketball could be played. We stayed there. Then later vehicles could be heard again and a group came in, another group of people. When it dawned ----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please, sir. Maybe this is a new night coming in and the next day things happen again. I think this would be, your Honours, a proper moment to give the witness a break and we might continue to listen to his story tomorrow morning. Thank you so far.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I think on behalf of my colleagues I could agree with you. So we can have a break now. The hearing is adjourned and we will start tomorrow at 10 o'clock.

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned for a short time).
(The court adjourned until the following day)
